cur:objects-weimar-liuthard-group-book-c.summary: At the top of this tall plaque Christ ascends in a mandorla toward the hand of God that reaches down from the clouds, flanked by angels. Beneath, the apostles look up in amazement around a central haloed figure with raised arms, and in the lowest register a crowd gathers before a gabled building within city walls. The swirling, agitated figures are typical of the Liuthard Group, the ivory carvers of Charles the Bald's court.
facts: The museum label attributes the cover to the Liuthard Group, named after the scribe Liuthard who worked for Charles the Bald, in the second half of the 9th century.
cur:objects-weimar-liuthard-group-book-c.notes: The subject of the lowest register could not be identified with confidence from the photograph.

cur:objects-essen-senkschmelz-cross.summary: Instead of a sculpted corpus, this jewelled cross carries five large enamel plaques; the central one shows the Crucifixion, with Christ on the cross between the Virgin and St John, while the enamels at the ends of the arms show the evangelist symbols. The intense blues, greens and whites of the enamel glow amid the gold and gems. It is counted among the masterpieces of Ottonian goldsmiths' work.
facts: Its name refers to its five unusually large plaques of senkschmelz ('sunk') enamel, in which the enamel sits in recesses surrounded by plain gold; the border also held 24 small enamels, 21 of which survive.
Its block-shaped arm ends resemble the cubic capitals popular in architecture around the year 1000.
